strength: Catches the top-5 run-out, rushes only those shades, stays inside ₹1.2 crore with arithmetic that checks out, and gives the ops lead a clean dated timeline that includes ad pause and order caps to stretch stock.
mistake: It counts the 3,900 held units as already inside the 9,100. It states this as an assumption, but it means re-cartoning doesn't extend the top-5 runway, so the gap and the rush quantity may be overstated.
to10: Settle whether held stock is extra to the 9,100, size the rush on that answer, and show the working for each shade's split.

strength: Shows the top-5 maths step by step (back-orders + sale at 2.5x + buffer), adds reorder points per line, and gives a Monday trigger sheet with owners, so ops can run it without guessing.
mistake: It also treats the held units as inside on-hand, so the re-cartoning win looks smaller than it may be. Its palette target of 3,000 sold by January barely dents ₹60 lakh of stuck cash.
to10: Settle the held-stock reading and set a more ambitious palette clearance plan that turns more of the ₹54 lakh of excess back into cash before January.

strength: It splits the 4.0 into brand versus non-brand (non-brand at 2.26, losing about $20,100 a month) and cuts all $146,300 of below-break-even spend outright, with a split that adds to exactly $240,000.
mistake: The plan is hard to follow in places: the $104,000 reserve and the separate regional test that brings back image and video spend need careful reading, and the 'products only, no images or video' PMax setup is stated more simply than Google allows in practice.
to10: Give a fuller price-mismatch diagnosis (sale_price, variant links, automatic item updates) and add the customer's own words, like 'eight hours', in search-facing copy.

strength: Excellent feed-fix steps (check page, feed and structured data; sale_price with dates; variant links; automatic item updates) plus customer-language titles and ad copy, with base and cautious profit cases that add up.
mistake: It keeps $128,000 in brand-excluded PMax with no explicit cut or negatives on 'women's flats' and 'sustainable shoes', even though its own cautious case runs PMax at 2.2, below break-even.
to10: Cut or exclude the 1.2 and 1.6 search categories directly, size PMax to the proven winners, and add explicit rules for cutting money in weeks two to four.

strength: A sharp decision up front with the cheapest fix first, honest ranges that credit the quiz with only half its 19-point gap, and a scan-conditioned day-3 message that never over-promises.
mistake: It never states the baseline cost of returns or tickets, and its post-delivery message only links to the quiz instead of helping a first-time bra buyer judge fit herself; the November and Christmas dates are an unstated assumption.
to10: Show the £139,800 and £31,360 baselines with a total saving, and add simple try-on fit tips for first-time bra buyers after delivery.

strength: It starts from the real cost base (£139,800 in returns, £31,360 in tickets), totals the saving at £11,830 to £19,770 with the working shown, and gives first-time bra buyers fit help: a pre-dispatch fit check plus try-on tips on delivery.
mistake: Message 4 says 'Still on track' even when the courier hasn't scanned the parcel, which risks a promise we can't keep, and the 5-day 'How's the fit?' nudge could add swap traffic that still costs £7.50 each.
to10: Send the day-3 message only after a courier scan, add a conversion guardrail on the fit-quiz button, and rank the three fixes explicitly by money saved.

strength: A tight, buildable one-screen flow: the pause comes back for 'no time', there is no discount for trip-enders, and the 'Email me in 3 or 6 months' box speaks straight to Greg's next-spring trip.
mistake: It keeps 50% off for switchers with no data behind it, and that row's £607 'after discount' is really close to full price (67 × £9), since half price would be about £300.
to10: Drop or test the switcher discount, fix its value, and give an honest range around the 1,400 lift instead of a single point.

strength: It opens with the decision, the lift with a range (+1,368, £11k a month, £98k per yearly group) and the hard truth that without the pause the flow keeps fewer than today, which makes rebuilding the pause the clear first task.
mistake: Trip-enders get a kind but plain exit with no 'remind me before your next trip' option, which leaves Greg's 'maybe next spring' unused, and 'It helps us help you' reads a little like a retention script.
to10: Add an opt-in reminder for trip-enders, tighten the copy to stay safely under 1,000 words, and keep a holdout on today's flow to prove the lift.

strength: A ranked plan built on tickets removed, three tight answer-first articles, and an honest range forecast with full working, plus a balances-screen banner idea priced in tickets and dollars.
mistake: It adds new articles rather than retitling the old ones or adding search synonyms. The existing 'How balances work' and 'Deleting expenses' titles still don't match what people search, and the restore article has no web steps.
to10: Retitle or add the search terms 'undo delete', 'restore expense' and 'recover deleted' so the 4,900 no-click searches land on the new article, and add web steps.

strength: The articles are more complete, with web steps, cancel-subscription steps and edit history, and it fixes the search mismatch both by retitling and by adding search terms.
mistake: It proposes merging 'Recording a payment', which already helps 71% of readers, and gives a single point forecast that includes week-2 currency savings rather than a true range.
to10: Drop the needless merge and present the forecast as a range with the currency article's contribution kept separate.

strength: It refuses the 20% cut with correct lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, $1,174 net) and a sharp break-even: lose 4 of the top 20 and the saving is gone.
mistake: It gives the Partner tier 40% for year one, which adds about $46,000 of rate cost on top of an open-ended 90-day window cost it never totals.
to10: Price the 90-day window as a total figure, compete for the top 20 on service and speed rather than rate, and put real dates and owners on the 30-day plan.

strength: It shows the honest cost: a cut on new referrals only saves about $38,000 in year one, and the 90-day window costs $62,000 to $89,000, worked from 3,365 customers and churn.
mistake: The rule 'we pay on new customers who keep their plan' is muddy next to the lifetime promise, and the 40% rival threat is answered only with service perks.
to10: Tighten that payout rule wording and add a fallback if a top-20 partner gets a firm 40% offer.

strength: It puts the money on the top-5 matte shades. Rush and standard orders are costed correctly at ₹117.46 lakh, with working shown, and re-cartoning is a Monday task. Back-orders with honest dates cover the December gap, and a pro pre-book idea is added.
mistake: It is dense and probably over the 900-word limit. The reorder-point table, the split formulas and the check sheet make it harder for an ops lead to scan. It also treats the 9,100 top-5 units as already including the held stock, so it never shows the 13,000 / 3.4-week effect of re-cartoning.
to10: Trim it to the word limit with one dated action list for Monday. Show the re-carton effect on top-5 cover. Add a short back-in-stock message in the brand voice for customers like Tanvi.

strength: It gives one clear plan. Costed POs total ₹1.187 crore and fit the cash. A dated action table runs from Monday to 15 Jan. Honest back-in-stock copy and a Farah pro pre-order protect the key customers without fake scarcity.
mistake: Pausing ads and capping orders at 4 per shade on the hero shades gives up sales and is blunt. Back-orders would keep that revenue. It also never shows the 13,000-unit / 3.4-week effect of re-cartoning, so it still sees a 1 to 8 Dec stockout.
to10: Show the stock position after re-carton and test whether back-orders beat the ad pause. Add a shade-level split instead of 'by sales share', and add a tighter glitter plan that recovers more than cost.

strength: It strips brand out of the 4.0 and shows each line's profit against the 2.5 break-even. The profit table is right and the split adds to exactly $240,000.
mistake: The forecast is optimistic. It assumes brand search jumps to about 25 ROAS, a brand-new non-brand Search campaign earns 3.2, and the reserve is fully spent. That gives a ROAS of 4.6 and +$61k of profit while PMax is cut by $82k.
to10: Use a defensible forecast with an honest range, including the likely fall in reported revenue. Add clear week 2 to 4 cut and scale rules, and put an owner and a done-when on each action.

strength: It shows that non-brand Google lost about $20k last month and that brand hides this inside the 4.0. It then gives a profit range, says plainly that reported revenue will fall, and sets explicit weekly reserve and cut rules.
mistake: The plan holds $104k in reserve and the base profit forecast assumes only the $136k committed is spent, so it can read as under-deploying the budget. The $61.9k feed upside is also a rough guess.
to10: Give a clearer base case for how much of the reserve is likely to be spent. Add a dedicated non-brand Search campaign for the washable and standing terms, and tighten the length.

strength: The numbers are rigorous and honest: it halves the fit-finder gap to allow for self-selection, builds a holdout and a conversion guardrail into the rollout, flags Christmas distortion, and adds a creative 'ship the swap first' option.
mistake: It gives only four messages and no fit coaching after delivery beyond a quiz link. It also mixes monthly and 90-day units, which makes the money harder to compare, and never states the baseline cost of returns and tickets.
to10: State the £139,800 and £31,360 baselines up front, add a real post-delivery fit-coaching message, and keep every saving in one unit ranked by gross profit.

strength: It opens with the cost baseline (£139,800 returns, £31,360 tickets, 6,076 day 3-5 tickets), then gives six short one-button messages, including fit-coaching copy at delivery and a day-5 fit check-in, and a table of savings with working in one unit.
mistake: It leans on an unproven 2-hour size-switch window before picking. The high case also assumes quiz users keep the full 14% return rate, and the £183,800 'sales kept' figure is a loose ceiling, though both are caveated.
to10: Show the swap-first portal's net gross-profit effect rather than a sales ceiling, drop the size-switch dependency from the core plan, and add one bolder idea beyond the standard flow.

strength: It retires the blanket discount and matches each reason to the right move: the pause for "no time", the 12-month switch for monthly payers, a kind exit for "trip over" and a reminder for "not progressing". It also says plainly that the pause does 80% of the work and the flow keeps fewer people than today's offer without it.
mistake: The "+£98k first year" and "£1.18m" figures multiply the monthly gain without a clear churn adjustment. The button reads "active once a reason is picked", which sits a little uneasily with always-visible, one-tap cancelling.
to10: Add a holdout or control cell to the measurement plan, apply churn explicitly to the annual figures, and drop the 'active once a reason is picked' wording so the cancel button is always live.

strength: The numbers are shown group by group (2,239 kept vs 842, about £11,340 more a month). The build notes are practical, including a 10% holdout on today's flow for 8 weeks.
mistake: It gives 50% off for 3 months to people switching apps, the same discount that 61% of takers abandon. It also adds a "smaller goal" offer with no data behind it, and it shows no range or risk on its guesses.
to10: Give a plain exit to the switchers instead of a discount, state a low-to-high range on the projection, and fill in the placeholders.

strength: It rewrites the main balances article around Jordan's question, with a hedged "probably" and an answer in the first lines. It also covers the currency gap in the plan and the forecast, and it shows the working.
mistake: The forecast is a single point estimate (3,743) with only a loose "half my shares" fallback, not a real range. The Android refund steps are vague, and the merge advice for "Recording a payment" is muddled.
to10: Give a proper low-to-high ticket range, tighten the Apple and Google steps, and add one bolder idea beyond the plan, such as an inline balance note with its risk.

strength: It opens with the decision and a ticket and dollar range, then gives a clear ranked table. Retitling and linking the delete article in searchers' own words is a cheap same-day fix, and a short "bad news" note says honestly that 2,000 refund tickets can't be removed.
mistake: It writes the Simplify article as a new page and only links to the old one, instead of rewriting "How balances work". It also states flatly that the group has Simplify turned on, and it leaves currency out of the forecast.
to10: Rewrite the existing balances article directly, hedge the Simplify claim, and trim the length to fit the 1,200-word cap.

strength: A straight no to the 20% cut, backed by the lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, net $1,174). It then costs the 90-day window honestly and says the plan costs more than today, with a dated 30-day plan the one partner manager can run.
mistake: Some figures are thin or unsupported: the '$38,000 if we cut only new referrals' line has no working, the window-cost projection rests on a guessed 65-75% pay-by-day-90 rate, and the length probably runs over 1,100 words.
to10: Show the working for the $38,000 figure, give a total plan cost against the finance saving, and say how the plan holds the top creators against the rival's 40% offer without a rate change.

strength: The numbers on the 20% cut are clear and correct: a 12.5% break-even, four top affiliates wiping out the saving, first-year commission at 20%, 30% and 40%, and lifetime value net of commission. It also answers the rival's 40% offer with a partner-tier rate.
mistake: The cost of the 90-day window is left vague ('may be the biggest cost', $63,000 per 10% rise) and no total plan cost is given. The 30-day plan uses day ranges instead of dates, and the $100 first-customer bonus nudges toward more recruiting.
to10: Add a total cost of the plan against the $210,000 saving, put calendar dates on the first 30 days, and spend the perk budget only on the top partners.

strength: A simple Monday plan: rush and standard orders for the top 5 shades, nothing for the slow lines, ₹1.19 crore total, plus an honest 'back on 9 December' message in our voice.
mistake: It assumes the 3,900 held units are already in the 9,100 on hand, so it misses that re-cartoning closes most of the pre-sale gap; it also cuts palettes to ₹699 from 1 December, which throws away margin early.
to10: Count the re-cartoned units as extra stock (about 13,000 for the top 5, lasting to about 8 December), and set the palette discount with a sales trigger instead of a blanket early cut.

strength: Shows the working for the rush and standard order sizes (back-orders plus sale week at 2.5 times plus buffer), with reorder points and a Monday check sheet the ops lead can actually run.
mistake: It makes the same wrong assumption that the held units are in the 9,100 on hand, so it overstates the 1 to 7 December gap; the back-order wording is also a bit flat for our voice.
to10: Treat the 3,900 re-cartoned top-5 units as added stock, and write the back-order message in our bold, playful voice.

strength: It splits the 4.0 ROAS into profit after ads for every segment against the 2.5 break-even, shows that non-brand Google loses about $20,100 a month, and names each loss-making line it cuts.
mistake: It holds $104,000 (43% of budget) in reserve and adds brand negatives to the 4.8 bags Shopping campaign, which could starve one of the real winners; some lines are cryptic, such as the unexplained $59,948.
to10: Put more of the reserve straight into the proven winners from day one, drop the brand negatives on bags, and explain jargon such as structured data and final URL expansion in plain words.

strength: A thorough feed fix that also stops it recurring (sale_price with dates, automatic item updates), plus title and Search ad copy built from Claire's and Nina's own words, with checked base and cautious profit cases.
mistake: It leaves $128,000 in brand-excluded Performance Max with no explicit negatives on 'women's flats' or 'sustainable shoes', relying on the target ROAS to fix a 2.0 campaign, and its 2.6 base-case ROAS looks optimistic.
to10: Explicitly cut the broad and sustainable terms and the display spend, and add clear week two to four rules for when to cut each line, not only when to release reserve.

strength: Tight, honest maths: it halves the 19-point fit-finder gap to allow for keen buyers self-selecting, and it flags that a Christmas run will distort results unless judged against a holdout.
mistake: The delivered message only links to the fit finder and gives first-time bra buyers no real fit help, and it never totals what the whole plan saves.
to10: Add a short post-delivery fit-check message for first-time bra buyers and a single total-savings line ranking the three fixes by money.

strength: Starts from where the money sits (£139,800 of returns, £31,360 of tickets) and adds practical bra fit guidance on delivery plus a day-5 'How's the fit?' nudge, which hits the fit problem before a return is booked.
mistake: The day-3 'Nearly there' message can fire before any courier scan, so the [tracking status] field may be empty or confusing. Six messages also stretches the 'short and few' principle.
to10: Send the day-3 message only after a courier scan (warehouse check otherwise) and add a Christmas or seasonality caveat to the expected numbers.

strength: It brings back the switched-off pause as the main save, shows the pause carries 80% of the result, and gives the working, an honest range and a first move this week.
mistake: The cancel button only becomes active once a reason is picked, and the 'trip over' group gets no 'remind me before your next trip' option.
to10: Keep the cancel button live from the start, add an optional 'remind me before my next trip' to the trip-over panel, and hold back a group on today's flow to prove the lift.

strength: Fine-grained panels: a remind-me email for trip-over, a smaller goal for learners who already have reminders, real local prices on the annual switch, and a 10% holdout to test the assumptions.
mistake: It keeps a 50% discount for app-switchers and counts those 67 discounted subscribers at full £9 'after discount', which overstates the value. The £136,000 year figure also ignores churn.
to10: Drop or justify the switcher discount, value discounted subscribers at the price they actually pay, apply churn to the yearly figure and give a range.

strength: It opens with the decision, an honest ticket range ($11,100 to $17,500 saved) and the bad news about the 2,000 Apple and Google refunds, then backs every number with working that checks out.
mistake: It writes a separate Simplify debts article and only edits the top of 'How balances work', so the 21,000-view page that only helps 38% of readers stays mostly broken. It also misses adding the 'undo delete' search terms to the help centre search.
to10: Rewrite 'How balances work' in place around Simplify debts, and map the 4,900 no-click searches to the restore article as search synonyms.

strength: The articles are the most complete: app and web restore steps, the Apple and Google cancel paths, and a cheap fix that adds 'undo delete', 'restore expense' and 'recover deleted' as search terms for the restore article.
mistake: The forecast is one number plus a half-shares floor rather than a reasoned range. It also counts the currency article as live mid-month and suggests merging 'Recording a payment' into a new page when that page already helps 71% of readers.
to10: Lead with the decision and an honest range, open the refund article with 'Ask Apple or Google' in the first line, and leave the 71%-helpful payment article alone.

strength: A straight no on the 20% cut, backed by lifetime maths, a break-even of 4 to 5 top partners, and the insight that a fair cut on new referrals only saves about $38,000. It pairs this with a dated 30-day plan the one partner manager can actually run.
mistake: The window-cost projection rests on a guessed 65 to 75% day-90 conversion, and the dense tables make the reasoning hard for a non-expert to follow.
to10: Explain the break-even and window-cost maths in a couple of plain sentences, and show a simple total for next year's net cost against today.

strength: The clearest explanation of why the cut fails. The 70 versus 80 cents break-even, losing four partners, and becoming the lowest payer are all easy for an owner to grasp and repeat to finance.
mistake: It adds a 40% first-year Partner rate (about $46,000) on top of the window cost when finance is asking for savings. The 30-day plan also has no real dates.
to10: Justify or drop the 40% Partner rate against the cheaper fixes, give the first 30 days real dates, and total the year's added cost in one line.

strength: The rush and standard orders for the top 5 shades are sized from the sale-week 2.5x demand and a named 6-day gap, and the total is ₹1.17 crore with checked arithmetic. It also spots that the draft sends 82% of matte money to shades that bring 42% of sales.
mistake: It runs well over 900 words and is dense with extras (a reorder-point table, a check sheet, a bolder pre-book idea), and it delays the standard order to 20 Nov with no reason given.
to10: Cut it to 900 words with one dated action list, place the standard order on Monday as well, and add a short on-brand back-in-stock message for Tanvi.

strength: It gives a tight plan the ops lead can run Monday: a PO table with dates, a dated action table, and an honest plan for the 1 to 8 Dec gap, with a notify message in the brand's voice that uses Tanvi's "wait a week" line.
mistake: It accepts a sell-out of the hero shades and pauses their ads. It also bundles the palette with kohl, a line it is buying, and clears palettes only at cost on 1 Feb, which recovers little cash.
to10: Keep the dated plan and add a stronger plan to turn the palette stock into cash, for example bundling it with the slow liquid lipsticks and releasing it earlier.

strength: It shows profit after ad cost for each line against the 2.5 break-even, puts the money into concrete winners (bags, a new non-brand Search campaign on Claire's searches), and gives a split of $240,000 that adds up with daily budgets.
mistake: Its forecast is too rosy (brand search at about 25 ROAS, profit up $61k, total ROAS 4.6), and it gives thin rules for weeks two to four beyond releasing a reserve.
to10: Use a more cautious forecast with a clear profit range, and add explicit week 2 to 4 rules for scaling and cutting, such as a 14-day PMax ROAS floor or a restore trigger.

strength: It combines brand search and PMax brand terms to show that non-brand Google ran at 2.26 and lost about $20,100, and it tells the owner the bad news (reported revenue falls about 13%) with a profit range and explicit assumptions.
mistake: It holds $104,000 in a rule-based reserve and expects $40,000 or more to go unspent, so it does not move the cut money into the winners decisively. The state-split test also adds complexity.
to10: Commit more of the reserve up front to the proven winners (washable and work-flat terms, bags) and add a dedicated non-brand Search line.

strength: It reasons honestly about the fit finder gap, crediting only half of the 19 points because keen buyers self-select. It backs this with a holdout, a fit-finder A/B test with a conversion guardrail, and a Christmas warning. The numbers all trace to the brief.
mistake: It sends only four messages and gives the fit help little room. The first-time bra fit nudge is a short block in the confirmation, and the only post-delivery help is a generic line in the delivered email, with no follow-up before a customer decides to return.
to10: Add a dedicated post-delivery fit message for first-time bra buyers, tighten the length, and use a cautious exchange target in place of the 35 to 45% jump.

strength: It opens with the cost base (£139,800 in returns, £31,360 in tickets), then gives six short one-button messages in the brand voice. The delivered and day-5 fit messages give practical fit tips and a swap button, which suits Jess and Amira.
mistake: The 10-minute fit-check email relies on a 2-hour order-edit window that may not exist. It also counts the £183,800 swap figure as sales kept, and it never states the fit-finder selection bias or the seasonal timing risk outright.
to10: Name the selection bias in the fit-finder estimate, allow for Christmas timing, and add a fallback for the size-switch window.

strength: A full, build-ready flow with exact copy for every reason and outcome. It brings the pause back for "no time" and gives goal-reached people a kind exit with a "remind me" option. The Cancel button is always live, and the maths ties out (842 vs 2,239 kept, about £11.3k a month more).
mistake: It gives a single point estimate with no honest range. It also leaves the 50% off in place for app-switchers and builds the reminder and annual-switch numbers on the discount's take rate without flagging how shaky that is.
to10: Add a low-to-high range on the untested offers and a plain warning that the flow depends on the pause, and cut the discount for the switching group or justify it with data.

strength: It leads with the money and the bad news. The pause does 80% of the work, and without it the flow keeps fewer than today. It gives a range (+1,230 to +1,680), names rebuilding the pause as this week's first move, and adds a measurement plan with a threshold.
mistake: The "goal reached or trip over" screen is a plain exit with no remind-me-later option. The Cancel button is inactive until a reason is picked, and the 12-month revenue figures rest on unexplained churn assumptions.
to10: Add a "remind me before my next trip" option on the trip-over screen, keep the Cancel button live at all times, and show the working behind the 12-month revenue numbers.

strength: The ranking is built on tickets that can be removed, with the working shown. The forecast is an honest range (2,700 to 4,300 fewer tickets, $11,100 to $17,500) whose arithmetic checks out, and it leads with the bad news about Apple and Google refunds.
mistake: It runs well over the 1,200-word limit, and it adds new articles beside the old ones instead of rewriting them, which leaves two overlapping balance pages and a thin plan for the week-2 pages.
to10: Cut it to 1,200 words, fold the 'bolder move' into the main plan, and make the new articles replace the old ones so the help centre has one page per task.

strength: The three articles are practical and complete: Simplify debts can be checked and turned off, restore steps cover app and web, and the refund article covers Apple, Google and web payments plus how to cancel. It also adds the search-term tip for the 4,900 unclicked searches.
mistake: The forecast is a single estimate of about 3,700 fewer tickets with only a 'half my shares' fallback, not a real range. It also plans to merge the 71%-helpful 'Recording a payment' article, which spends effort where the data shows little gain, and it never links the Settle up screen.
to10: Give a proper low-to-high forecast, drop the low-value merge, link the Settle up screen, and bring it under the 1,200-word limit.

strength: A straight 'no' to the 20% cut, with correct lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, $1,174 net after commission) and a 40%-for-year-one Partner tier that answers the rival threat with a costed figure.
mistake: The first-30-days plan has no dates or owners, and the 'four people can wipe it out' break-even argument is loosely argued; the plan also runs over the 1,100-word limit.
to10: Use dated, owned steps for the first 30 days, tighten the break-even logic, cut to the word limit, and add one fresh idea beyond tiers and perks.

strength: A decisive 'no' to the cut with the lifetime maths, honest about the plan costing more than today, and a dated, owner-assigned 30-day plan that one partner manager can run, led by calling the top 20 by name.
mistake: The window-cost projection and the '$38,000 cut-only-new-referrals' figure rest on thinly explained assumptions, and the plan runs over the word limit.
to10: Show the working for the $38,000 and the 65–75% day-90 assumption, trim to the word limit, and say how the top 20 are protected from a rival's 40% offer.

strength: Shows its working, and the maths checks out: 24,000 rush sized from back-orders plus sale week at 2.5x plus a buffer, an exact ₹117.46 lakh total, and the 82%-of-matte-money-to-42%-of-sales critique of the draft.
mistake: It counts the 6,400 held units as already on hand, so it concludes the top 5 still run out on 1 December and plans a back-order gap that re-cartoning might close; that assumption isn't challenged.
to10: Settle whether held stock adds to the 9,100, and add a single dated day-by-day timeline for the ops lead instead of dates spread across several tables.

strength: A single dated action calendar the ops lead can run on Monday, plus smart gap tactics (ad pause, per-shade cap, pro pre-order, honest 'back on 9 December' copy that uses Tanvi's 'I'll wait a week').
mistake: Same held-stock assumption creates a 1 to 8 December gap. Pausing top-5 ads from 16 November gives up sales while stock still exists, and the liquid lipstick leftover (~27,900) doesn't quite reconcile with plain run-rate.
to10: Test whether re-cartoned stock extends cover to the rush arrival, and time the ad pause and cap to a stock trigger rather than day one.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart against the 2.5 break-even, and every profit, budget and forecast number checks out: $36,708 lost in non-brand PMax, a split that totals exactly $240,000, and $1,114,700 base value.
mistake: It keeps $128,000 in PMax and forecasts a 2.2 cautious case, which is below break-even, and adds no negatives to stop the 1.2 broad and 1.6 sustainable spend from leaking back in.
to10: Add negatives for broad and sustainable terms, move PMax to products only, and set explicit week 2–4 cut and scale rules with a new-customer guardrail.

strength: It cuts exactly the $146,300 of loss-making spend and backs that with concrete PMax mechanics: brand exclusion, negatives, products only, and final URL expansion off. It adds week-by-week rules, a new-customer guardrail, owners for each step, and a costed regional test of whether broad spend builds brand.
mistake: The $198,000 profit forecast doesn't show how much of the $104,000 reserve it assumes gets spent, and parking that much unspent may look to the CFO like an underspent plan.
to10: Show the line-by-line working behind the $198,000 profit forecast, and add search ad or asset copy built on Claire's 'stand in for eight hours' language.

strength: Every cost figure checks against the brief (£139,800 in returns, 6,076 day 3–5 tickets, 540–1,080 fewer bra returns, a £11,830–£19,770 total), and there are two bra-specific fit messages after delivery that help before a return.
mistake: Message 4 says 'still on track' even when the courier has not scanned the parcel, which risks a promise we cannot keep. The 23.5% low case is never explained as an adjustment for the type of buyer who uses the quiz.
to10: Send the day-3 update only after a courier scan, say why the fit gain is halved, and name owners and a conversion guardrail for moving the quiz.

strength: Sharp, honest reasoning. strength: Takes the 4.0 ROAS apart against the 2.5 break-even, puts the 212-variant feed fix first, and moves the cut money into bags and the customer's-words terms inside a $240,000 split that adds up.
